presidents.name: Chester A. Arthur
trivia: Took the presidential oath in New York City after Garfield died, then took it again in Washington—the first to be sworn in privately at home like that.
Signed the Pendleton Civil Service Act (1883), creating competitive exams for many federal jobs instead of pure patronage.
Before reform, he was a leader in New York’s Republican patronage machine under Senator Roscoe Conkling.
Never won a presidential election of his own; Republicans refused to renominate him in 1884.
Nicknamed “Elegant Arthur” for expensive clothes and polished manners unusual for a machine politician.
Hired designer Louis Comfort Tiffany to redecorate the White House in lavish Gilded Age style.
Political enemies claimed he was born in Canada so he would be ineligible for the presidency; he was born in Vermont.
Signed the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882), the first major U.S. law to ban immigration by a specific nationality.
Suffered from Bright’s disease (a kidney illness) and kept how sick he was mostly secret while in office.
Often the forgotten name between Garfield and Cleveland in “list the presidents” pub rounds.
Pub-trivia shorthand: the dandy who takes over after Garfield and unexpectedly passes civil-service reform.

presidents.name: Grover Cleveland
trivia: First Democrat elected president after the Civil War.
Only president to serve two nonconsecutive terms—he is counted as both #22 and #24.
Only president married in the White House; he wed 21-year-old Frances Folsom in 1886.
Vetoed more bills than any president before him, earning a reputation for using the “veto pen.”
Had secret surgery for jaw cancer aboard a yacht in New York Harbor so the public would not panic markets.
Won the popular vote in 1884, 1888, and 1892, but lost the 1888 Electoral College to Benjamin Harrison.
During the 1884 campaign, opponents chanted “Ma, ma, where’s my pa?” over an alleged illegitimate child; supporters answered “Gone to the White House, ha, ha, ha!”
Born Stephen Grover Cleveland and dropped his first name in public life.
Elected reform mayor of Buffalo and governor of New York before winning the presidency.
His nonconsecutive terms are the model for later “same person, two numbers” trivia (like Trump as 45 and 47).
Pub-trivia shorthand: nonconsecutive-terms guy (also #24); first Democrat after the Civil War; White House wedding.

presidents.name: Benjamin Harrison
trivia: First president to have electric lights installed in the White House.
First president to have his voice recorded on a phonograph.
Only grandson of a president to become president (grandson of William Henry Harrison).
Signed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), the first federal law to limit monopolies.
Six new states entered the Union during his term: North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Washington, Idaho, and Wyoming.
Lost the 1888 popular vote to Grover Cleveland but won the Electoral College; Cleveland beat him in the 1892 rematch.
Nicknamed the “Human Iceberg” because he seemed cold and stiff in public.
He and First Lady Caroline Harrison were reportedly uneasy about electric switches, so staff often turned the lights on and off for them.
Served as a Union brigadier general from Indiana in the Civil War.
Hosted the first Pan-American Conference, an early push for diplomacy among nations in the Americas.
Pub-trivia shorthand: William Henry Harrison’s grandson; electric lights in the White House; Sherman Antitrust Act.

presidents.name: Grover Cleveland
trivia: Only person counted as two different numbered presidents (#22 and #24).
His daughter Esther Cleveland was the first child of a sitting president born in the White House.
His second term opened with the Panic of 1893, a severe depression with bank failures and mass unemployment.
Sent federal troops to Chicago to break the 1894 Pullman Strike, saying it blocked U.S. mail delivery.
Defended the gold standard against “free silver” Democrats, splitting his party before William Jennings Bryan’s rise.
The Baby Ruth candy bar was marketed as named for his daughter Ruth Cleveland, though many people assume it was for slugger Babe Ruth.
Together with his first term, he is the only pre-21st-century example of nonconsecutive presidential terms.
In 1893 doctors removed a cancerous growth from his mouth on a yacht; the operation stayed secret from newspapers for years.
Left office unpopular with many Democrats who wanted easier money and more aid during the depression.
Same person as president #22—quiz questions often ask why the numbering skips or doubles.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Cleveland’s second time around—same man as #22; Panic of 1893 and Pullman Strike.

presidents.name: William McKinley
trivia: Last Civil War veteran to serve as president.
Third president assassinated; anarchist Leon Czolgosz shot him at Buffalo’s Pan-American Exposition in 1901.
President during the Spanish–American War (1898); the U.S. took Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
Annexed Hawaii as a U.S. territory in 1898.
Ran a “front porch campaign” from Canton, Ohio, where crowds came to hear him instead of him barnstorming the country.
Campaign manager Mark Hanna raised huge corporate donations and is often called an early architect of modern campaign finance.
Built his brand on high protective tariffs and “full dinner pail” prosperity after the 1890s depression.
His death made Vice President Theodore Roosevelt, at 42, the youngest person ever to become president.
First Lady Ida McKinley had epilepsy; he was known for quietly covering for her seizures at public events.
Died eight days after being shot, after an initially hopeful recovery turned to gangrene.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Spanish–American War president; annexes Hawaii; assassinated → Teddy becomes president.

presidents.name: Theodore Roosevelt
trivia: Youngest person ever to become president (age 42) after McKinley’s assassination.
First president to fly in an airplane—as a former president in 1910, at a St. Louis air meet.
First president to ride in an automobile, and first sitting president to travel outside the United States (to Panama).
First American to win a Nobel Peace Prize, for mediating the end of the Russo-Japanese War (1905).
Trust-buster who used the Sherman Antitrust Act against monopolies and signed the Pure Food and Drug Act after muckraking exposés.
Created or expanded many national parks, forests, and monuments as a leading conservation president.
Led the Rough Riders volunteer cavalry in the Spanish–American War; the teddy bear is named for a hunting story about him.
One of the four faces on Mount Rushmore.
Ran for president again in 1912 on the Progressive “Bull Moose” ticket, splitting Republicans and electing Woodrow Wilson.
In 1912 a would-be assassin shot him in the chest; he gave a lengthy campaign speech before going to the hospital.
Pub-trivia shorthand: youngest president; Rough Riders / teddy bear / big stick; first to fly (as ex-president).

presidents.name: William Howard Taft
trivia: Only person to serve as both U.S. president and Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.
First president to throw out a ceremonial first pitch at a Major League Baseball game.
Heaviest president (over 300 pounds); the White House installed an oversized bathtub large enough for him.
Handpicked by Theodore Roosevelt as successor, then became Roosevelt’s rival when TR ran as a third-party candidate in 1912.
His Justice Department filed more antitrust lawsuits than Roosevelt’s, despite Taft’s milder public image.
Said he preferred being Chief Justice to being president; Harding appointed him to the Court in 1921.
A famous story claims he got stuck in a White House bathtub—likely exaggerated, but tied forever to his size.
Served as governor-general of the Philippines before becoming secretary of war and then president.
Yale graduate who later chaired the effort that designed the Supreme Court Building.
Finished third in the 1912 popular vote behind Wilson and Roosevelt after the Republican split.
Pub-trivia shorthand: only president who later becomes Chief Justice; bathtub / baseball first-pitch guy; TR’s rival in 1912.

presidents.name: Woodrow Wilson
trivia: Only U.S. president with a Ph.D.; he had been president of Princeton University.
First president to hold regular presidential press conferences.
Asked Congress to declare war in 1917 and proposed the Fourteen Points and a League of Nations after World War I.
Signed the Federal Reserve Act (1913) creating the modern central bank, and the Clayton Antitrust Act.
Suffered a severe stroke in 1919; First Lady Edith Wilson tightly controlled who could see him afterward.
Won 1912 because Taft and Theodore Roosevelt split the Republican vote; won 1916 on “He kept us out of war.”
Ordered segregation of several federal government offices, rolling back integrated workplaces.
The Senate rejected U.S. membership in the League of Nations despite his national speaking tour for it.
His portrait appeared on the rare $100,000 gold certificate used only for transactions between Federal Reserve banks.
Last president born in a state that had joined the Confederacy (Staunton, Virginia).
Pub-trivia shorthand: WWI president; League of Nations; only Ph.D. president; stroke covers-up with Edith.

presidents.name: Warren G. Harding
trivia: First president elected after the 19th Amendment gave women the national right to vote (1920).
First president whose voice was broadcast over radio (a 1922 speech).
Won with the slogan “Return to Normalcy,” promising calm after World War I and progressive upheaval.
Died in office in San Francisco in 1923; afterward the Teapot Dome scandal showed Cabinet members had taken bribes for oil leases.
Owned and edited the Marion Star newspaper in Marion, Ohio before entering politics.
Nominated in a hotel “smoke-filled room” compromise at the 1920 Republican convention after the convention deadlocked.
After his death, Nan Britton claimed a long affair and a child with him—one of several sex scandals tied to his circle.
His poker-playing, Prohibition-era White House social scene became a symbol of cronyism.
Often ranked near the bottom of presidential lists because of corruption among friends he appointed.
First sitting president to visit Alaska, on the western trip during which he fell fatally ill.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Return to Normalcy”; Teapot Dome; dies in office → Coolidge takes over.

presidents.name: Calvin Coolidge
trivia: Only president born on the Fourth of July (July 4, 1872).
First president to make a radio address from the White House.
First president whose inauguration was broadcast on radio, and an early star of talking newsreels.
After Harding died, Coolidge’s father—a Vermont notary—swore him in by kerosene lamp at the family home in Plymouth Notch.
Nicknamed “Silent Cal” for saying as little as possible in conversation.
A dinner guest bet she could get him to say more than two words; he answered, “You lose.”
Presided over much of the 1920s boom with a small-government, pro-business approach.
Could likely have won in 1928 but chose not to run for another full term (“I do not choose to run”).
Kept a pet raccoon named Rebecca that lived at the White House for a time.
As Massachusetts governor, broke the 1919 Boston police strike by calling out the state guard and refusing to rehire strikers.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Silent Cal”; sworn in by his dad on a Vermont farm; Roaring Twenties president.
